claim: Use a swipe to trigger a primary action only when the app can also expose that action through a visible control or a long-press menu — never let a gesture be the sole path to functionality.
why: Gestures are invisible; a user who never discovers the swipe is locked out of the feature entirely, whereas a redundant button costs only screen space.
when: Replacing or supplementing a tap target on list rows, cards, or item collections.
fails: The redundant control clutters a dense layout — in that case keep the gesture plus a discoverable affordance like a peek or hint animation rather than dropping the fallback silently.

claim: Reuse the same motion vocabulary for a gesture that you already established elsewhere in the product — if horizontal card paging uses a particular easing and travel distance, the swipe-to-add interaction should animate identically.
why: Repeating a motion signature teaches the gesture once and lets the learning transfer, so the second interaction feels familiar on first encounter.
when: Adding a new gesture to an app that already has an established swipe or drag pattern.

claim: Make bottom sheets and modals dismissible by dragging them in the direction they entered from — a sheet that slid up from the bottom should be draggable down to close.
why: The entry animation implicitly teaches the exit gesture; direction of arrival sets the user's spatial expectation for where the panel goes when it leaves.
when: Any overlay presented from a screen edge — bottom sheets, side drawers, full-screen covers.
fails: The sheet's content scrolls vertically; the drag-to-dismiss must then only engage when the inner scroll is already at the top, or scrolling will fight dismissal.

claim: Animate the underlying screen when a sheet appears: scale it down slightly and translate it away from the sheet, then reverse exactly on dismissal.
why: Moving the background makes the overlay read as a physical layer stacked in front of the page rather than a flat rectangle pasted on top, and it visually confirms that the page is still there waiting underneath.
when: Modal sheets and popovers that cover part of the screen and return the user to the same context on close.
fails: Full-screen navigation pushes where the previous screen genuinely leaves the stack — the background recede reads as a lie if the user isn't coming back.

claim: Always ship a visible close or dismiss button on a sheet even when drag-to-dismiss works.
why: The gesture is faster for users who know it, but the button guarantees an exit for those who don't and for anyone who can't perform a precise drag.
when: Every dismissible overlay.

claim: Gate irreversible or high-consequence actions behind a slide-to-confirm control that requires dragging a handle the full width of the track, rather than a single tap on a button.
why: A sustained directional drag is far harder to perform by accident than a tap, so the input itself encodes deliberate intent and removes the need for a separate confirmation dialog.
when: Sending, publishing, purchasing, transferring funds, deleting — anything with no undo or real-world cost.
fails: Routine, reversible, or frequently repeated actions, where the added friction becomes a tax; also poor for users with limited motor control unless a tap alternative exists.

claim: Require the slider to travel the entire track before firing, and snap it back to origin if released early.
why: A partial-travel threshold reintroduces the accidental-trigger risk the control exists to eliminate; the full traverse is what makes the commitment unambiguous.
when: Slide-to-confirm components.

claim: Prefer gestures over buttons where speed of repeated interaction matters, and prefer buttons where the action is rare or destructive — match input cost to action frequency and reversibility.
why: Gestures optimise for fluency once learned; buttons optimise for discoverability and precision. The action's profile decides which trade-off is right.
when: Choosing the interaction model for any new action in a mobile app.

claim: When porting a desktop app to mobile, first try to reduce the sidebar to 3–5 top-level destinations and render them as a bottom navigation bar; cap it at five and aim for three or four.
why: The thumb-reachable bottom edge only fits a handful of items before each target shrinks below a comfortable tap size and the labels become unreadable.
when: The product's information architecture has a small set of genuinely top-level sections.
fails: The sidebar contains many equally important destinations that cannot be collapsed without burying real functionality — then a bottom bar forces arbitrary demotion.

claim: Keep every navigation touch target at least 44×44px, and let the item count drive the layout rather than shrinking items to fit more in.
why: Fingers are imprecise contact patches, not cursors; below roughly 44px the mis-tap rate climbs sharply.
when: Any tappable element, especially dense rows of navigation icons.

claim: Break the single most important action out of the bottom bar — elevate it as a distinct centre or offset button rather than treating it as one more equal tab.
why: Navigation and creation are different intents; giving the primary action its own visual weight stops it competing with destination switching.
when: The app has one dominant create/compose/add action.

claim: Float the bottom bar above the content with margin around it instead of pinning it edge-to-edge as a full-width slab.
why: The floating treatment reads as current-generation mobile styling and visually separates the chrome from scrolling content.
when: Modern consumer app UI where the bar sits over scrollable content.

claim: Treat bottom-bar and top-bar contents as page-dependent: swap secondary items for actions relevant to the current screen rather than freezing one global set.
why: A fixed global bar wastes prime screen real estate on items irrelevant to what the user is currently doing.
when: Screens with meaningfully different task contexts (a document view vs. a list view).
fails: The primary destination tabs — those should stay stable so users don't lose their spatial map.

claim: When the sidebar won't compress, convert it into a full-screen navigation page that doubles as the app's home screen.
why: A whole page can hold the full hierarchy at readable sizes, so nothing has to be demoted into a hidden overflow menu.
when: Content-heavy or workspace apps with deep, wide navigation trees.
fails: Apps where users mostly ping-pong between two or three views — a nav home page adds a hop to every switch.

claim: A nav-as-home page made of one left-aligned link list will look lopsided; balance it by adding a recents/recently-viewed block at the top and right-aligning per-row metadata such as counts and quick actions.
why: A single column of short labels leaves the right half of the screen empty; pushing counts and actions to the right edge activates that space and makes the rows scan as complete units.
when: Any full-page list-based navigation hub.

claim: With navigation moved to a full page, reclaim the freed bottom edge for a large persistent search field or primary action button.
why: The bottom strip is the most thumb-accessible zone; if tabs aren't using it, the highest-frequency action should.
when: The nav-as-home-page pattern, where search or capture is a top user task.

claim: Default the top bar to a notification bell plus an overflow menu, then layer on screen-specific actions from there.
why: It's a safe baseline that covers global alerts and low-frequency settings without pre-committing screen space.
when: Early layout blocking, before per-screen requirements are known.
fails: Later stages, where the top bar should be re-derived from what the specific page actually needs.

claim: Do not scale desktop type and spacing down for mobile; keep them the same or increase them, and treat ~17px as the mobile body-text floor versus ~13px on desktop.
why: Mobile devices are held closer but viewed in worse conditions — motion, glare, one-handed use, thumbs as pointers — so legibility and touch targets need more absolute size, not less, even though the canvas shrinks.
when: Adapting an existing desktop layout to phone screens, or picking a base font size and spacing scale for a new mobile app.
fails: Dense data surfaces that users deliberately scan at length — spreadsheets, trading terminals, code editors — where a compact scale is the point and users accept the legibility cost.

claim: When a desktop screen contains several parallel modules, pick exactly one to be the mobile screen's subject and move the rest to separate screens, tabs, or sheets.
why: With type held at or above desktop size and far less area available, there is only room for one module's worth of content; trying to keep all of them forces the compression that made the layout unreadable in the first place.
when: Porting a multi-pane desktop view (sidebar + list + detail + secondary panels) to a phone.

claim: Judge a mobile layout's density by placing it side by side with mainstream apps at 1:1 scale rather than evaluating it on its own.
why: An over-compressed screen looks internally consistent and therefore fine in isolation; the error only becomes legible against a reference whose scale users already have calibrated expectations for.
when: Reviewing your own mobile mockups, especially when you have been staring at them zoomed in on a large monitor.
fails: Comparison apps drawn from a different category with different density conventions — a dense finance app is not a fair reference for a reading app.

claim: Take platform default values — system base font size, standard spacing units, default control heights — as the starting scale for a platform rather than porting a scale across platforms.
why: Platform defaults encode the vendor's own testing for that viewing distance and input method, so they are a calibrated baseline; each platform's numbers differ for reasons specific to how that device is used.
when: Beginning a design on a platform whose conventions you have not internalised.
fails: Strongly branded products with a deliberate typographic voice, where defaults are a floor for legibility rather than a prescription for style.

claim: Zoom your mobile artboard to physical device size before judging spacing, and check it on an actual handset before shipping.
why: Working zoomed in on a desktop display makes cramped padding and undersized text look generous, which is what produces the squeezed layout that seems normal until compared.
when: Any phone-sized design work done in a desktop design tool.

claim: For each mobile content section, choose one primary movement direction: a vertical stack or a horizontally scrollable row.
why: A phone screen cannot comfortably present the same two-dimensional grid structure that desktop dashboards can.
when: Adapting dense desktop or dashboard content to a mobile interface.
fails: A deliberately specialized interaction genuinely requires nested two-axis navigation, which is not addressed in the chapter.

claim: Build mobile screens from cards, text or links, images, and inputs, combining these elements inside cards when a grouped unit is useful.
why: This small set of primitives covers most app content while keeping layouts flexible.
when: Composing standard mobile application views.

claim: Use cards to group related content when whitespace alone cannot establish a clear relationship.
why: Cards create bounded content groups in space-constrained mobile layouts.
when: Related information or actions need a shared visual unit.

claim: Avoid nesting cards inside cards unless the hierarchy cannot be expressed another way.
why: Each card adds padding, so nested containers consume usable width and make the interface feel cramped.
when: Designing dense mobile content areas with multiple grouped elements.
fails: A nested container provides necessary hierarchy or interaction separation and sufficient space remains.

claim: Prefer whitespace-based grouping over an additional container when it communicates the relationship clearly.
why: It preserves content area while reducing unnecessary visual and spacing overhead.
when: Adjacent elements need light grouping rather than a strong boundary.
fails: Whitespace alone does not make grouping, hierarchy, or interaction boundaries clear enough.

claim: When a screen slides in from the right on a back gesture, do not leave the underlying screen static — translate it in the opposite direction by roughly a third of the screen width and animate it back to zero as the gesture completes.
why: Two layers moving at different rates read as parallax, which tells the eye the screens are stacked in depth rather than swapped flatly; a static background looks like a slideshow.
when: Push/pop navigation stacks where the previous screen sits conceptually behind the current one.
fails: Root-level or peer screens with no parent-child relationship — implying depth where none exists misleads the user about where they are.

claim: Drive the back-transition offsets directly from finger position rather than firing a fixed-duration animation on gesture release.
why: A gesture that tracks the finger 1:1 lets the user preview and abort the navigation; a canned animation makes the swipe a mere trigger and breaks the sense of direct manipulation.
when: Any interruptible, reversible navigation gesture.
fails: Gestures whose outcome is not reversible or has no meaningful intermediate state.

claim: For bottom sheets, express depth by scaling the background down slightly as the sheet rises and scaling it back up as it dismisses, instead of translating it.
why: Scale reads as the background receding away from the viewer, which is the correct spatial metaphor for a sheet arriving in front of it; horizontal motion would imply lateral navigation.
when: Modal or semi-modal sheets that rise over the current context and return to it.
fails: Non-modal or persistent sheets where the background stays interactive — shrinking it signals the content behind is unreachable.

claim: Choose the axis of the background's reaction to match the axis of the incoming layer: opposing horizontal translation for horizontal navigation, scale for vertical overlays.
why: The background's response is the user's cue about what kind of transition just happened; mismatching the axis makes navigation and modality feel interchangeable.
when: Designing the counter-animation for any layered transition.

claim: Only lean on a swipe as a primary path to a feature if you have shipped some means of teaching it — a first-run hint, a visible affordance, or a widely established platform convention.
why: Swipes leave no persistent visual trace, so an untaught swipe is a feature that a share of users will never find; once learned, though, it is faster than any button.
when: Assigning meaningful functionality (search, archive, back) to swipe gestures.
fails: Destructive or hard-to-reverse actions, where a hidden gesture risks accidental invocation without a confirmation step.

claim: Offer a swipe-up-to-search shortcut on primary screens where search is a frequent task, since it borrows recognition from OS-level and mainstream app precedent.
why: Reusing a gesture users have already learned from the operating system and popular apps removes most of the discoverability cost of a hidden interaction.
when: Content-heavy apps where search is a high-frequency destination.
fails: Screens where a vertical swipe already owns another behaviour, such as scrolling lists or pull-to-refresh, which would conflict.

claim: Treat long press as the mobile equivalent of right-click: reserve it for secondary and contextual actions on an object, never as the only way to reach a primary action.
why: It maps onto a mental model users already hold from desktop, keeping the primary tap free for the object's main behaviour.
when: Any list item, card, message, or tile that has more actions than fit inline.
fails: Primary actions, which must remain reachable by tap for discoverability and accessibility.

claim: Build the long-press menu from three simultaneous moves: blur and dim the rest of the screen, scale the pressed element up slightly so it lifts off the surface, and render the action list adjacent to it.
why: The blur removes competing context, the lift identifies exactly which object the actions belong to, and the pairing keeps the menu anchored to its target rather than floating free.
when: Contextual action menus invoked by long press on a specific element.
fails: Very dense grids where scaling the element would push it under the finger or off-screen; the lift needs surrounding room.

claim: For media or content items, upgrade the long-press state from a static thumbnail into an enlarged live preview of the item alongside the actions.
why: The preview turns the menu into a peek at the destination, so a long press becomes a useful action on its own even when the user picks nothing from the list.
when: Items whose content is worth previewing — photos, links, messages, videos.
fails: Items with no meaningful visual payload, where an enlarged preview adds latency and motion without information.

claim: Treat a mobile screen's action chrome as mode-dependent: on entering a focused task, hide the global navigation and replace it with only the actions that operate on the object in view.
why: Phone viewports can't hold a global nav plus a full task toolbar without crowding out the content; swapping rather than stacking keeps the visible controls relevant and the content area intact.
when: Drilling from a list or home surface into an editor, detail, or task view where a distinct set of operations becomes available.
fails: Users need to jump between top-level sections while working — hiding global nav with no cheap way back (a back affordance or dismissible mode) strands them.

claim: For a modal, committal step like picking a template or confirming a choice, strip the interface down to two controls: one to accept and one to cancel out.
why: A step with exactly one decision should present exactly that decision; any other control is a chance to lose the user's place or their in-progress selection.
when: Short, self-contained flows where the user is making a single choice before returning to the main task.
fails: The step actually needs secondary operations (preview, filter, search across options) — forcing it down to two buttons then hides functionality the task requires.

claim: Anchor task-specific action bars to the top edge when they replace a bottom navigation bar, so the two chrome layers don't compete for the same screen region.
why: Reusing the bottom slot for a different action set makes the swap read as a glitch; placing editing tools at the top keeps each region's meaning stable — bottom means 'where am I', top means 'what can I do here'.
when: Apps with a persistent bottom tab bar that also need contextual toolbars in detail views.
fails: One-handed-reach-critical actions get pushed to the top of a tall device where the thumb can't comfortably reach them.

claim: Animate action sets in and out of the chrome rather than hard-cutting them, so the user can see that controls were replaced rather than that the screen was rebuilt.
why: A transition that shows old controls leaving and new ones arriving preserves the sense of a continuous space and teaches the mode change; an instant swap reads as a discontinuity the user has to re-parse.
when: Any mode change that alters which actions are visible in persistent chrome.

claim: Derive which actions to show from the object currently in focus, not from a fixed per-screen list — a note in view means formatting and sharing, a picker in view means confirm and dismiss.
why: Scoping actions to the focused object is what makes a small screen feel like it has enough room; the user only ever sees the operations that could apply right now.
when: Designing the toolbar or app-bar contents for any content-editing or content-selection surface.
fails: Actions that users expect to be globally reachable (search, new item, account) get buried inside object-scoped chrome.

claim: When designing a desktop app, treat conformance to the host platform's conventions as the primary UX goal — match the OS's native layout, chrome, and interaction patterns rather than porting a web layout into a window.
why: Users arrive with an existing mental model built from every other app on their machine; matching it means the interface needs no learning, while deviating from it makes the app read as a foreign object regardless of how polished it is in isolation.
when: Building an app that will be installed and run alongside first-party apps on a specific OS (here, macOS), where the user's baseline expectation is set by the system's own software.
fails: Not addressed in this chapter. (Cross-platform products, or brand-forward creative tools that intentionally define their own environment, would trade native conformance for consistency or identity.)

claim: Budget design effort across three layers — overall window layout, composition within each region, and the small platform-specific interaction details — and treat the third layer as required, not polish.
why: The narration singles out subtle OS-level interactions as the thing that separates a convincing desktop app from a web page in a window, implying the perceived nativeness lives in details that are easy to skip.
when: Planning the scope of work for a desktop app design, deciding what to cut under time pressure.

claim: For utility apps whose job is capture or lookup, make the primary entry point a global keyboard shortcut and design the window to dismiss itself immediately after the task completes.
why: The user is always mid-task in another app when the need arises; forcing an app switch costs more attention than the task itself is worth.
when: Single-purpose tools invoked frequently and briefly — clipboard managers, capture inboxes, launchers, quick-search.
fails: Apps the user deliberately sits inside for long sessions (editors, browsers, IDEs), where a persistent window and normal window chrome are correct.

claim: Derive the invocation and dismissal model from what the user is doing immediately before and after they need your app, not from the app's own feature list.
why: The surrounding workflow determines whether an app switch is acceptable; designing from features alone produces a destination when the moment calls for an overlay.
when: Deciding entry points, window type, and exit behaviour early in a product's design.

claim: Strip window chrome that implies persistence — remove traffic-light controls from transient overlay windows and rely on the shortcut plus auto-dismiss for lifecycle.
why: Close/minimise/zoom controls signal a window meant to be managed and kept around; an overlay that vanishes on completion has no lifecycle for the user to manage.
when: Floating, shortcut-invoked panels that close on task completion.
fails: Any window the user may want to resize, park alongside other content, or return to later — removing chrome there strands them without a visible exit.

claim: Cut an overlay's contents to the minimum needed for one task: one input affordance, one drop target, and only the actions that complete or cancel.
why: Every extra control adds a decision to a moment the user wants to spend under two seconds in.
when: Transient capture or command surfaces.
fails: Interfaces where the user needs to browse, compare, or edit what they've already captured — that belongs in a separate, fuller window.

claim: Label action buttons with their keyboard equivalents inline so the shortcut path is learnable from the UI itself.
why: A shortcut-first app is only fast once the shortcuts are known; showing them on the button teaches them during ordinary mouse use.
when: Any surface where keyboard operation is the intended fast path.

claim: Use a translucent blurred background material on floating panels so the overlay reads as a system layer sitting above the user's work rather than an opaque foreign window.
why: Blur preserves the context underneath and matches the material vocabulary the OS uses for its own transient surfaces.
when: Floating panels, popovers, and edge-anchored widgets on macOS.
fails: Content requiring precise colour judgement or dense reading, where a busy backdrop showing through hurts legibility.

claim: Give the dismissal its own animated transition — collapse the panel into a small confirmation element that then exits the screen — instead of cutting it to nothing.
why: The animation carries the confirmation, so the user learns the action succeeded without a separate dialog or a return trip to the app.
when: Submit-and-vanish interactions in transient overlays.
fails: Failure-prone or destructive actions where an animated success would misreport the outcome.

claim: Adopt optimistic UI for save-and-dismiss actions: update the interface as though the operation succeeded, then perform the upload, write, or sync in the background.
why: The user's confidence in the result matters more than confirmation of it; waiting on the network to close a two-second interaction destroys the point of the overlay.
when: High-success-rate operations that are recoverable if they fail — saving, filing, moving, deleting to a recoverable location.
fails: Operations that are irreversible, likely to fail, or where the user acts on the assumed result — payments, permanent deletion, publishing. Optimistic UI also requires a real failure path that surfaces and retries the error.

claim: Anchor transient surfaces to a screen edge or let them be repositioned, rather than pinning them to the centre of the display.
why: The user's real work is on screen underneath; an unmovable centred panel occludes exactly what they were referring to.
when: Overlays, edge widgets, and quick-entry panels.

claim: Before designing a novel interaction, name one or two native or well-regarded apps that already solve the same moment, and inherit their invocation, placement, and dismissal conventions.
why: Users judge nativeness against patterns they already have muscle memory for; borrowing a proven pattern buys familiarity for free.
when: Introducing any interaction outside the standard document window.

claim: Before choosing a layout, classify the surface as content-presentation or content-hosting; design a hosting surface around the shape and volume of what the user will put into it, not around what looks good filled with sample copy.
why: A page ships with its content baked in and can be composed around it; an app's content arrives later, in unpredictable quantity, and the interface's job is to survive that variation.
when: Starting any app window, dashboard, or editor where the substance on screen is created or collected by the user.
fails: Marketing sites, onboarding flows, docs, and other surfaces where the content is authored once and fixed — there, composing tightly around the specific content is correct.

claim: Default a desktop app window to three zones: a top bar for actions that apply to the whole app, a left sidebar for switching between sections, and the remaining area for content.
why: It is the convention users have already learned from the system's own utility apps, so navigation costs them nothing to figure out.
when: Multi-section desktop apps on macOS, or anywhere users expect platform-native behaviour.
fails: Single-purpose apps with one or two destinations — the sidebar becomes an empty rail that costs width and returns nothing.

claim: Cut the sidebar when the app has fewer than roughly three top-level destinations, and reallocate the freed horizontal space to the content itself.
why: Navigation chrome earns its footprint only in proportion to how much there is to navigate; unearned chrome shrinks the thing users came for.
when: Apps whose entire navigation reduces to browsing one collection plus filtering or searching it.
fails: The app is likely to grow more sections later — retrofitting a sidebar forces a full relayout, so plan for it if growth is expected.

claim: Keep the top ~50px of a macOS window free of dense controls so the window-drag region stays usable.
why: That strip is how users move the window; filling it with buttons removes an interaction the OS guarantees everywhere else.
when: Any custom-chrome macOS window, particularly ones with a full-width toolbar.

claim: Place the traffic-light buttons inside a real UI region — the toolbar or the top of the sidebar — and space the surrounding elements to that same rhythm, instead of leaving a blank strip above your layout to accommodate them.
why: Treating them as ordinary elements in the grid removes the seam between system chrome and app content, which is what makes native apps read as one surface.
when: macOS apps using a custom or unified toolbar.

claim: Hide controls that operate on content until content exists — show filters, sort, bulk actions, and view switchers only once there is something for them to act on.
why: A control that cannot do anything yet is noise that the user has to read and dismiss before understanding what the app is for.
when: First-run and empty states in any collection-based app.
fails: Controls whose absence would hide the app's capabilities entirely, or where appearing later causes a jarring layout shift — reveal those with a disabled state or a stable slot instead.

claim: Design the empty state as a single prompt toward the one action that ends it, rather than as a decorated placeholder.
why: With nothing on screen, the empty state is the entire interface, so it should carry exactly one instruction.
when: Any app whose main view starts out with zero items.

claim: Show each item's summary in the browsing view and defer its full metadata to an explicit selection or detail view.
why: Attaching every field to every item in a grid turns a scannable collection into a wall of text; the user asks for detail by clicking.
when: Grids, lists, and galleries where items carry more attributes than can be read at a glance.
fails: One or two attributes are the primary basis for choosing between items — those belong in the browsing view, not behind a click.

claim: Before adding colour, shadows, gradients, or any effect, state the minimum set of UI elements required for the content to be usable, and build that first.
why: Styling applied to a layout that is still carrying unnecessary elements just makes the unnecessary elements prettier.
when: The transition from wireframe to visual design on any content-heavy app.
fails: Products where the styling is itself the value proposition — a theme, a creative tool, a brand-led experience.

claim: Scope an app to one job, and let that scope be the argument for rejecting features that would need new navigation.
why: The layouts being copied are simple because the apps behind them are; a narrow feature set is the precondition for a narrow UI, not a consequence of it.
when: Deciding feature scope early, or defending against feature creep that would force a sidebar or tab bar into a simple app.

claim: Make search a permanently visible, top-level element of the main window rather than something behind a keyboard shortcut or nested menu.
why: Every first-party macOS app the user already knows exposes search prominently, so hiding it violates the platform's learned expectation and makes the feature feel absent.
when: Building a Mac app whose primary content is a browsable collection of items.
fails: Content sets small enough to scan at a glance, where a persistent search field is chrome that buys nothing.

claim: Choose the search pattern that preserves your app's navigation model: if the app is meant to live on one screen, keep results in an overlay or side panel instead of a command palette that swaps the whole view.
why: A command palette is a navigation device — it takes the user somewhere else. Adopting it inside a single-screen utility imports a multi-screen mental model the rest of the app doesn't support.
when: Deciding between a modal command palette, an inline filter, and a floating field with an attached results surface.
fails: Apps that genuinely span many screens, documents, or workspaces, where jumping to a destination is the point and a palette is the right tool.

claim: Evaluate a borrowed UI pattern against your app's architecture, not against how polished it looks in the app you saw it in.
why: Patterns carry structural assumptions with them; a pattern can be well-designed and still be wrong for a product with a different shape.
when: Any time a pattern is adopted because a well-regarded product uses it.

claim: When search can match on content rather than titles, design the query field for descriptive natural-language phrases — long, multi-clause input, not one-word keywords.
why: Content-aware matching invites queries like 'mobile app with houses and a calendar', which need field width, sensible placeholder copy, and no assumption of short tokens.
when: Search is backed by image recognition, embeddings, or any semantic index over the item contents.
fails: Purely lexical filename or metadata search, where descriptive phrasing will return nothing and misleads the user about capability.

claim: For visual libraries, show a small set of the most relevant matches per item in a secondary panel rather than dumping a full flat result list.
why: Truncating to a few strong results per item keeps the panel scannable and communicates relevance ranking instead of raw recall.
when: Results are images or other visual artifacts and each source item can produce multiple matches.
fails: Tasks requiring exhaustive review, where silently hiding matches causes the user to miss things.

claim: If your search results view looks visually similar to your default browse view, add explicit state markers so the user can always tell which one they are looking at.
why: Two near-identical screens with different meanings is a disorientation bug; the user loses track of whether the grid is everything or a filtered subset.
when: Search filters in place and reuses the browse layout, grid, or card components.
fails: Search opens a visually distinct surface, where the difference is already self-evident and extra chrome is redundant.

claim: Ship four affordances with any in-place search state: a result count, a one-click clear, the active query echoed persistently in the interface, and an explicit path back to unfiltered browsing.
why: Count answers 'did this work and how much matched', clear and back offer two exit routes at different costs, and the echoed query keeps the filter visible after the field loses focus.
when: Search results replace or filter the primary content area.

claim: Put the result count and clear control inside the search bar itself, and the query label with a back arrow at the top-left of the content area.
why: Status about the query belongs with the input that produced it; navigation out of the filtered state belongs where the platform already trains users to look for back controls.
when: Laying out a floating search bar over a content grid.

claim: Make every content item in the app a valid drag source, so a user can pull it out into any other app without an export step.
why: Export dialogs and save flows force the user to model where the app's data lives; a drag lets them move content by direct manipulation, which costs no learning.
when: Desktop apps that hold discrete content units — images, links, files, notes, clips — that a user plausibly wants to use somewhere else.
fails: Items that are references rather than content (a live query, a permissioned record), where the receiving app would get a broken or meaningless payload; those need an explicit export with format choice.

claim: Support drag and drop in both directions, and treat drag-out as the harder requirement — most apps implement drop-to-import and stop there.
why: Getting content in is a one-time setup cost the user tolerates; getting content out is the repeated act, so friction there compounds across every session.
when: Any app that stores user content and sits in a workflow alongside other tools.

claim: Accept drops on the app's primary capture surface, not on a separate import screen — the window the user already has open should be the drop target.
why: A dedicated import mode adds a navigation step before the content transfer that the user came to perform.
when: Apps with a quick-entry or quick-save window as the main input path.

claim: Ship the platform share affordance alongside drag, rather than choosing one — drag wins when both windows are visible, share wins when the destination is not on screen.
why: Dragging requires the target to be reachable; a share sheet works with a hidden or backgrounded destination, so the two cover complementary situations.
when: Any app where users send content to destinations outside the current screen arrangement.

claim: Put the frequent actions for an item — copy, locate, delete — in a floating bar pinned inside the detail or preview panel, rather than only in a menu bar or context menu.
why: Actions used on nearly every item should cost one click from where the user is already looking; burying them behind a right-click or a top-level menu adds a discovery step each time.
when: Detail views, preview panels, and slide-outs where a small, stable set of operations applies to the currently shown item.
fails: When the action set is long or varies per item type — a floating bar of many buttons becomes visual noise and should collapse to an overflow or context menu.

claim: Reuse the same floating-overlay treatment for every persistent control cluster in the app (search, actions), so the user learns one visual convention for 'this floats above the content and is always available'.
why: A repeated form teaches its own meaning; a second floating element in a different style reads as an unrelated component and has to be learned separately.
when: Apps that already use one floating overlay control and are adding a second.

claim: Use this test on an interaction: if the user would have to consciously remember it exists, redesign it; the target is behaviour they attempt on instinct and find works.
why: Features the user must recall compete for attention; behaviours that match existing expectations cost nothing to use.
when: Evaluating whether an interaction pattern is worth shipping or needs a different affordance.
fails: Genuinely novel capabilities with no existing mental model still need visible teaching — the criterion applies to standard operations, not to new ones.

claim: Anchor interaction decisions to what the platform's first-party apps already do, since those set the user's baseline expectation for the OS.
why: Users arrive having learned the system apps' behaviour; matching it means the app requires no new learning, while deviating reads as broken.
when: Building for a platform with a strong, consistent set of built-in apps.

claim: Ship a first-run onboarding moment in desktop apps, not just mobile ones — especially when the app's primary interface is invisible until a shortcut summons it.
why: A desktop utility whose main surface is a hidden panel gives the user no discoverable affordance to poke at; without a first-run explanation the app appears to do nothing.
when: Building a menu-bar, background, or shortcut-invoked desktop app where the core UI is not visible on launch.
fails: The app's function is fully visible and self-evident in a window on launch, where a modal just adds a click before the user reaches the thing they can already see.

claim: Make the onboarding modal's only dismissal action be performing the shortcut it just taught, rather than an 'OK' or 'Got it' button.
why: Executing the shortcut once turns a read instruction into a rehearsed motor action, and the panel appearing on success is immediate confirmation the user did it right.
when: Teaching a single critical invocation gesture — a global hotkey, a swipe, a drag — that the whole app depends on.
fails: The gesture is unavailable or blocked (shortcut conflicts with another app, missing accessibility permission, hardware without the key), so always provide an escape hatch rather than trapping the user in an undismissable modal.

claim: Give every keyboard shortcut a permanent, in-app reference sheet the user can reopen at any time — treat first-run teaching and ongoing lookup as two separate jobs.
why: Shortcuts are powerful precisely because they are invisible, and invisible things get forgotten; onboarding fires once, so it cannot serve as the user's long-term memory.
when: Any app that meaningfully rewards keyboard-driven use.

claim: Put the shortcut cheat sheet somewhere the user can reach without knowing a shortcut — e.g. inside the visible settings surface — and optionally also bind a shortcut to it.
why: A reference gated solely behind a hotkey is unreachable by exactly the user who has forgotten the hotkeys; the narration flags this circularity as ironic rather than as a model to copy blindly.
when: Deciding where discovery aids live in a keyboard-heavy app.
fails: In apps where a persistent visible chrome (menu bar item, toolbar) already lists shortcuts inline, a separate sheet is redundant.

claim: Scale onboarding to the app's surface area: a single-purpose utility earns one modal, not a multi-screen guided tour.
why: Onboarding length should be proportional to how much the user must know before the app is useful; over-onboarding a one-shortcut tool spends the user's attention on nothing.
when: Choosing onboarding depth for a focused tool with one or two core actions.
fails: Multi-mode or workflow-heavy apps where one modal cannot cover the concepts the user needs before first success.

claim: Invest the onboarding modal's polish budget in micro-interactions — animated transitions, responsive feedback on the shortcut firing — since it is the user's first impression of the app's craft.
why: The first-run screen is seen by every user exactly once and sets the perceived quality bar for everything after it.
when: Building the first-run experience of a consumer-facing desktop app aiming for an Apple-grade feel.
fails: Animation that delays the user's first successful action, or that replays on every launch, becomes friction rather than delight.

claim: Collect low-frequency configuration — shortcut reference, panel edge/anchor position, light/dark appearance — into one compact settings popover rather than a full preferences window.
why: A small utility has too few settings to justify a separate window; a popover keeps configuration adjacent to the app's actual surface and preserves the lightweight feel.
when: Menu-bar or panel-style macOS apps with a handful of preferences.
fails: Settings counts grow past what fits without scrolling or tabbing, at which point a real preferences window is the correct container.

claim: Expose the screen edge the panel slides out from as a user setting instead of hardcoding one side.
why: Panel position interacts with the user's physical setup — multi-monitor arrangement, dock placement, handedness — which the designer cannot know in advance.
when: Any app with a panel, drawer, or HUD that animates in from a screen edge.

claim: Offer explicit light/dark appearance control alongside system-follow rather than relying on the system setting alone.
why: Users of a persistent overlay utility often want it to differ from their system-wide appearance for contrast against whatever they're working over.
when: macOS apps that render over arbitrary other application content.
fails: Apps that should feel like a native, invisible extension of the OS, where diverging from the system appearance looks broken.

claim: Do not elevate a single tab-bar item into a raised circular FAB unless that action is genuinely the most-used destination; put it inline with the other icons instead.
why: Visual prominence should track usage frequency. The raised button steals hierarchy from the four tabs people actually navigate with, and it breaks the row's alignment.
when: Designing a bottom tab bar where one item is a content-creation or primary action shortcut.
fails: The app really is creation-first (a camera or capture app) where that one action dominates every session — then the emphasis is earned.

claim: Give every tab-bar item, including a create/add action, a defined active state — don't leave any item permanently in one visual mode.
why: If one item can never look selected, the bar's state model is inconsistent and that item reads as an outsider rather than a peer destination.
when: A tab bar where an item opens a full screen or modal that the user can be 'in'.
fails: The item fires a transient action that never becomes a persistent screen; there is no state to be in.

claim: Choose glyphs that have a distinguishable filled/outline pair so active and inactive states can be expressed without changing the icon's silhouette.
why: A symbol like a bare plus has no natural filled counterpart, which forces the designer to break the state system or leave that tab stateless.
when: Selecting an icon set for a navigation bar that uses fill-swap to indicate selection.

claim: Keep inactive tab icons at legible contrast against their background — do not dim them to the point of ambiguity.
why: The active indicator already communicates where the user is, so the inactive items don't have to be suppressed; they still have to be readable as destinations.
when: Any navigation bar that distinguishes active from inactive via colour or fill.

claim: Rely on more than one channel to signal the active tab: fill, weight, or colour on the icon itself rather than a background colour swap behind it.
why: Subtle background-tint differences are effectively invisible at tab-bar scale and on real screens, so the signal doesn't survive contact with users.
when: Indicating selection inside a compact horizontal bar.

claim: Spend your saturated brand colour on the active state of a nav item, not across the whole bar.
why: One accented element in an otherwise neutral bar reads as an intentional indicator; brand colour spread everywhere becomes noise and destroys the contrast you need for state.
when: You want the navigation to carry brand personality.

claim: Distribute tab icons toward the outer edges of the bar rather than clustering them centrally, so each item's tap region grows.
why: The tappable area of a tab is the full cell it occupies, so wider spacing means more forgiving thumb targets even when the icon glyph stays the same size.
when: Bottom navigation on touch devices with 3–5 items.
fails: Very wide screens or tablets, where fully edge-to-edge distribution puts items out of thumb reach.

claim: Add text labels under tab icons when the icons are not near-universal; omit them only when every glyph is a widely recognised convention.
why: Icon comprehension is learned. Familiar shapes (home, search, profile) survive alone; domain-specific or abstract glyphs do not, and the label is the cheap fix.
when: Deciding between icon-only and icon-plus-label bottom navigation.
fails: Vertical space is severely constrained, or the icon set is entirely conventional and the extra text just adds clutter.

claim: Apply the same contrast standard to tab labels as to any body text — never set them in a low-opacity grey that disappears against the bar.
why: A label added for clarity that can't be read adds height and clutter without delivering the comprehension benefit it exists for.
when: Any labelled navigation bar.

claim: Substitute the user's uploaded avatar for the generic profile glyph in the account tab when one exists.
why: A personal image is recognised faster than a generic silhouette and makes the destination unambiguously 'you'.
when: Apps with user accounts and profile photos.
fails: No avatar uploaded — fall back to the glyph or initials; also needs a treatment for the active state since a photo can't fill/unfill.

claim: Fix structure, contrast, and state before adding surface effects like translucency and blur; treat those as the final styling pass.
why: Blur and transparency reduce effective contrast, so they can only be layered safely on top of a bar whose legibility already has headroom.
when: Producing a stylised or dark-mode variant of a working navigation component.
fails: Content scrolling beneath is high-contrast or busy — the blurred bar then needs an added scrim or opacity floor.

claim: Put the primary outcome-driving action in the lower thumb-reach zone and keep it visible throughout the experience.
why: A share action is central to Wrapped’s social distribution, while top-aligned controls are harder to reach one-handed.
when: Designing full-screen mobile stories, recaps, or media flows with a dominant conversion action.
fails: The lower area is occupied by mandatory system navigation, gesture affordances, or content controls of higher priority.

claim: Design the available screen area for the actual platform rather than inheriting browser-layout constraints.
why: A native app does not need to preserve space for a mobile browser address bar, allowing safer use of the lower edge for controls.
when: The experience is delivered solely in a native app.
fails: The same layout must work in a mobile browser or other environments with obstructive browser UI.

claim: Combine controls when one action can provide the needed state change instead of adding a dedicated button.
why: Opening sharing can pause the currently playing story, so a separate pause affordance adds unnecessary interface weight.
when: Entering a secondary flow should temporarily stop or suspend media and that behavior is predictable to users.
fails: Users need to pause without sharing, or opening the secondary flow should not interrupt playback.

claim: Remove controls that duplicate well-established interaction patterns for the target audience.
why: The chapter treats tap-to-pause as a familiar story/video convention, making a visible pause button redundant.
when: The audience reliably recognizes the gesture and the gesture is discoverable within the product’s interaction model.
fails: The gesture is unfamiliar, inaccessible, conflicts with other taps, or the audience needs explicit playback controls.

claim: Separate persistent utility controls by reach and urgency: keep dismiss at the top, but place frequently adjusted controls near the bottom.
why: Closing is an infrequent escape action, whereas audio adjustment benefits from easy access during playback.
when: A full-screen media interface has both an exit control and ongoing playback utilities.
fails: Platform conventions, accessibility requirements, or visual safety zones require another placement.

claim: Make the primary repeat action available through a large, direct gesture target that requires minimal pointer or thumb travel.
why: Large targets and short movement distances make repeated actions faster and easier to perform.
when: A mobile product has one dominant, high-frequency action such as advancing through a feed or media sequence.
fails: When the gesture could conflict with important controls or users need deliberate, precise navigation.

claim: Place high-frequency mobile controls inside the comfortable one-handed thumb-reach area, adapting placement to the expected handedness of the audience.
why: Controls within the natural reach zone reduce physical effort during repeated use.
when: Designing phone interfaces whose primary audience predominantly uses one hand.
fails: A product must equally optimize for left- and right-handed use, or controls need to remain reachable across device sizes.

claim: Use automatic transitions such as snapping and autoplay to eliminate unnecessary steps between successive pieces of content.
why: Removing pauses and manual activation makes continuous consumption more efficient.
when: Content is intended to be consumed sequentially with low decision cost.
fails: Users need time, consent, or control before the next item starts; unchecked automation can reduce agency and create unwanted overuse.

claim: Treat low interaction friction, compelling short-form content, and strong personalization as a reinforcing system rather than isolated features.
why: Together they lower the effort to continue while increasing the chance that the next item feels relevant.
when: Designing an engagement-oriented personalized content feed.
fails: The product goal is intentional, bounded use rather than maximizing continued consumption.
